title: SQL fundamentals
intro: A relational database stores structured data in tables and lets you query that data with SQL. In this lesson, you will learn the SQL operations you need for the task manager, from simple SELECT queries through filtering, aggregation and your first JOINs.
body:
## What is a relational database?

A **relational database** stores data in tables. A table is made up of rows and columns, with each column describing a particular piece of information.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Tables linked by keys", "nodes": [{"id": "c", "label": "customers", "sub": "id PK · name · email", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "o", "label": "orders", "sub": "id PK · customer_id FK · total", "kind": "db", "highlight": true}, {"id": "i", "label": "order_items", "sub": "order_id FK · product_id FK · qty", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "p", "label": "products", "sub": "id PK · name · price", "kind": "db", "col": 1}], "edges": [{"from": "c", "to": "o", "label": "1 → many"}, {"from": "o", "to": "i", "label": "1 → many"}, {"from": "p", "to": "i", "label": "1 → many"}]}
~~~

For our task manager, we might have a `users` table:

~~~text
users
+----+--------+
| id | name   |
+----+--------+
| 1  | Anna   |
| 2  | David  |
+----+--------+
~~~

Each row represents one user. Each column represents an attribute of that user.

A column also has a **data type**. For example, an ID might be an integer and a name might be text.

Another table could store tasks:

~~~text
tasks
+----+---------+-------------------+------+
| id | user_id | title             | done |
+----+---------+-------------------+------+
| 1  | 1       | Learn SQL         | 0    |
| 2  | 1       | Build API         | 1    |
| 3  | 2       | Write tests       | 0    |
+----+---------+-------------------+------+
~~~

The `user_id` column connects a task to a user. This relationship is one of the key ideas behind relational databases.

## Why PostgreSQL?

This course uses **PostgreSQL** in production because it is a mature, powerful open-source relational database with strong SQL support and features that work well for Spring Boot applications.

PostgreSQL supports transactions, constraints, indexes, JSON data, sophisticated queries and many other capabilities. It is also widely used in professional backend systems.

We will use PostgreSQL for the actual task manager application. The exercises in this course run in SQLite in your browser, so you can practise SQL without installing a database. SQLite understands the fundamental SQL operations used in these exercises, although PostgreSQL has additional features and some syntax differences.

## SELECT: reading data

The most basic SQL operation is `SELECT`.

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "Written order vs. run order", "caption": "You write SELECT first, but the database evaluates it near the end — that is why WHERE cannot use a column alias.", "steps": [{"label": "FROM / JOIN", "sub": "which rows exist"}, {"label": "WHERE", "sub": "filter rows"}, {"label": "GROUP BY", "sub": "make groups"}, {"label": "HAVING", "sub": "filter groups"}, {"label": "SELECT", "sub": "pick columns"}, {"label": "ORDER BY · LIMIT", "sub": "sort and cut"}]}
~~~

~~~sql
SELECT name
FROM users;
~~~

This asks the database to return the `name` column from every row in `users`.

You can select multiple columns:

~~~sql
SELECT id, name
FROM users;
~~~

Avoid using `SELECT *` in application queries unless you genuinely need every column. Explicit column lists make it clear what the query needs and avoid accidentally returning newly added columns later.

For example:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title, done
FROM tasks;
~~~

## WHERE: filtering rows

`WHERE` restricts which rows are returned.

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE done = 0;
~~~

This returns open tasks in our exercise schema.

You can compare values with operators such as `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE id > 5;
~~~

### AND and OR

Combine conditions with `AND`:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE done = 0
  AND user_id = 2;
~~~

Both conditions must be true.

With `OR`, either condition can match:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE done = 1
   OR user_id = 2;
~~~

When combining `AND` and `OR`, parentheses make your intention explicit:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE done = 0
  AND (user_id = 1 OR user_id = 2);
~~~

## IN

`IN` is convenient when comparing a value with several possible values.

Instead of:

~~~sql
WHERE user_id = 1 OR user_id = 2 OR user_id = 3
~~~

you can write:

~~~sql
WHERE user_id IN (1, 2, 3)
~~~

This is especially useful when a filter contains a known set of values.

## LIKE

`LIKE` performs pattern matching on text.

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE title LIKE '%SQL%';
~~~

The `%` wildcard represents any sequence of characters.

For example, `%SQL%` can match `Learn SQL`, `SQL fundamentals` and `Advanced SQL queries`.

The exact behaviour of pattern matching can differ between database systems, particularly around case sensitivity, so check PostgreSQL's documentation when you need database-specific behaviour.

## IS NULL

SQL has a special value called `NULL`. It represents missing or unknown data.

You cannot correctly check for NULL with:

~~~sql
WHERE due_date = NULL
~~~

Instead, use:

~~~sql
WHERE due_date IS NULL
~~~

To find rows where a value exists:

~~~sql
WHERE due_date IS NOT NULL
~~~

This distinction is extremely important when writing database queries.

## ORDER BY

SQL does not guarantee a useful ordering unless you explicitly request one.

Use `ORDER BY`:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
ORDER BY title ASC;
~~~

`ASC` means ascending. `DESC` means descending.

You can sort by multiple columns:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title, done
FROM tasks
ORDER BY done ASC, title ASC;
~~~

The database sorts by `done` first and then uses `title` to break ties.

## LIMIT and OFFSET

For a large result set, you often want only one page of results.

`LIMIT` restricts the number of rows:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20;
~~~

`OFFSET` skips rows before returning results:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;
~~~

This can represent a simple second page of 20 results.

For production APIs, pagination has more details to consider, especially when data changes between requests, but `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` are useful fundamentals.

## INSERT: creating rows

Use `INSERT` to add data.

~~~sql
INSERT INTO users (name)
VALUES ('Anna');
~~~

For multiple rows, PostgreSQL supports:

~~~sql
INSERT INTO users (name)
VALUES ('Anna'), ('David'), ('Maria');
~~~

When writing application code, values should normally be supplied as parameters rather than concatenated into SQL strings. This protects against SQL injection and lets the database driver handle values correctly.

## UPDATE: changing rows

Use `UPDATE` to modify existing rows.

~~~sql
UPDATE tasks
SET done = 1
WHERE id = 5;
~~~

The `WHERE` clause is extremely important.

Without it:

~~~sql
UPDATE tasks
SET done = 1;
~~~

Every task in the table can be changed.

A useful habit when writing a destructive query is to first write the corresponding `SELECT`:

~~~sql
SELECT *
FROM tasks
WHERE id = 5;
~~~

Check that it identifies exactly the rows you intend to change, then write the `UPDATE`.

## DELETE: removing rows

`DELETE` removes rows:

~~~sql
DELETE FROM tasks
WHERE id = 5;
~~~

Again, forgetting `WHERE` is dangerous:

~~~sql
DELETE FROM tasks;
~~~

This can delete every row in the table.

The same principle applies to both `UPDATE` and `DELETE`: **always think about which rows the statement affects before executing it.**

## Aggregate functions

SQL can calculate values across multiple rows using **aggregate functions**.

Common aggregate functions include:

- `COUNT()` counts rows or values.
- `SUM()` adds numeric values.
- `AVG()` calculates an average.
- `MIN()` finds the smallest value.
- `MAX()` finds the largest value.

For example:

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM tasks;
~~~

Count open tasks:

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM tasks
WHERE done = 0;
~~~

You can give calculated columns useful names with aliases:

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS open_tasks
FROM tasks
WHERE done = 0;
~~~

## GROUP BY

`GROUP BY` lets you calculate aggregates separately for groups.

For example, count tasks for each user:

~~~sql
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS task_count
FROM tasks
GROUP BY user_id;
~~~

Instead of one total for the entire table, the database produces one result row per `user_id`.

You can calculate multiple aggregates at once:

~~~sql
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) AS task_count,
       SUM(done) AS completed_count
FROM tasks
GROUP BY user_id;
~~~

With our exercise data, `done` is represented as `0` or `1`, so the sum of `done` counts completed tasks.

## HAVING

`WHERE` filters individual rows before grouping. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.

For example, find users with at least three tasks:

~~~sql
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS task_count
FROM tasks
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
~~~

A useful mental model is:

~~~text
FROM
 ↓
WHERE
 ↓
GROUP BY
 ↓
HAVING
 ↓
SELECT
 ↓
ORDER BY
 ↓
LIMIT / OFFSET
~~~

The actual SQL execution process is more nuanced, but this model helps you understand the role of each clause.

## Your first INNER JOIN

A `JOIN` combines rows from related tables.

~~~widget sql-join
~~~

Suppose `tasks.user_id` points to `users.id`. We can retrieve the user name alongside each task:

~~~sql
SELECT users.name, tasks.title
FROM users
INNER JOIN tasks ON tasks.user_id = users.id;
~~~

An **INNER JOIN** returns only rows where the join condition matches.

If a user has no tasks, that user does not appear in this result.

You can use table aliases to make the query shorter:

~~~sql
SELECT u.name, t.title
FROM users AS u
INNER JOIN tasks AS t ON t.user_id = u.id;
~~~

This is the style you will commonly see in real SQL.

## LEFT JOIN

Sometimes you need all users, including users who have no tasks.

Use a `LEFT JOIN`:

~~~sql
SELECT u.name, t.title
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN tasks AS t ON t.user_id = u.id;
~~~

The left side of a `LEFT JOIN` is preserved. Every user appears, even if no matching task exists.

For a user without a task, the task columns contain `NULL`.

This distinction is important for our task manager. If you want a report containing every user and their task count, including users with zero tasks, a `LEFT JOIN` is usually the right starting point.

## NULL and aggregates

`NULL` can make aggregate queries surprising at first.

Consider a left join:

~~~sql
SELECT u.name, COUNT(t.id) AS task_count
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN tasks AS t ON t.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
~~~

For a user with no tasks, `t.id` is `NULL`. `COUNT(t.id)` does not count that NULL value, so the result is `0`.

This is different from `COUNT(*)`, which counts the joined result row itself. With a `LEFT JOIN`, `COUNT(*)` can therefore produce `1` for a user with no matching task.

That is why choosing what you count matters.

You will use this distinction in the exercise at the end of the lesson.

## Running PostgreSQL locally

When you work with the real task manager, PostgreSQL will run as your database server.

One common command-line client is `psql`.

For example, after PostgreSQL is installed and a database exists, you might connect with:

~~~shell
psql -h localhost -U postgres -d task_manager
~~~

The exact username, database name and authentication configuration depend on your local setup.

Inside `psql`, you can run SQL directly:

~~~sql
SELECT id, name
FROM users;
~~~

You can also use a graphical database client such as DBeaver. A GUI can make it easier to inspect tables, run queries and examine results while learning.

IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition does **not** include the database tools available in IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate, so do not expect the built-in database browser or SQL console from tutorials aimed at Ultimate users. Use `psql`, DBeaver or another PostgreSQL client instead.

## SQLite in the exercises

The SQL exercises in this course run against a fresh SQLite database in the browser.

The goal is to practise the SQL concepts rather than database administration. The exercises therefore use common SQL that works in both SQLite and PostgreSQL where possible.

There are differences between the systems. PostgreSQL has more data types, extensions, functions and database-specific features than SQLite. When you move your query into the real Spring Boot application, always check the PostgreSQL behaviour and syntax you need.

For the fundamentals in this lesson, the important concepts are the same: tables, rows, columns, filtering, ordering, grouping and joins.

## Common mistakes

### Forgetting WHERE on UPDATE or DELETE

This is one of the most dangerous beginner mistakes. Always check which rows your condition matches before modifying or deleting data.

### Using = NULL

`NULL` is not compared with `=`. Use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

### Using INNER JOIN when you need zero-count rows

An inner join removes users with no matching tasks. Use `LEFT JOIN` when every user needs to remain in the result.

### Counting the wrong thing

With a `LEFT JOIN`, `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(task.id)` can produce different results. To count matching tasks, counting a nullable task column such as `t.id` is usually what you want.

### Assuming result order

A query without `ORDER BY` does not promise a particular order. If your API or report requires a specific order, state it explicitly.

### Selecting every column by default

`SELECT *` is convenient while exploring a database, but application queries should normally request the columns they actually need.

### Confusing WHERE and HAVING

`WHERE` filters rows before grouping. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.

## A useful SQL mental model

Most queries you write for the task manager will combine a small number of building blocks:

~~~sql
SELECT columns
FROM table
JOIN related_table ON condition
WHERE row_conditions
GROUP BY grouping_columns
HAVING group_conditions
ORDER BY sort_columns
LIMIT number OFFSET number;
~~~

You will not always need every clause. A simple query may only need `SELECT`, `FROM` and `WHERE`.

As requirements become more interesting, you add joins, aggregation, ordering or pagination.

The next lesson will build on these fundamentals by designing a proper relational schema. You will learn about primary keys, foreign keys, relationships and constraints, then use those ideas to design the database behind the task manager.
takeaways: Relational databases organise structured data into tables containing rows and typed columns.
SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET form the foundation of everyday data retrieval.
UPDATE and DELETE require particular care because forgetting WHERE can affect every row.
GROUP BY and aggregate functions calculate summaries, while HAVING filters the resulting groups.
INNER JOIN returns matching rows, while LEFT JOIN preserves rows from the left table even without a match.

quiz.question: Which SQL condition correctly finds tasks that do not have a due date?
quiz.explanation: SQL uses IS NULL to test whether a value is NULL. Equality with NULL does not work as a normal comparison.

quiz.question:
What is the main difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN in this example?

SELECT u.name, t.title
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN tasks t ON t.user_id = u.id;
options: LEFT JOIN includes users even when they have no matching tasks
LEFT JOIN only includes users who have tasks
INNER JOIN always returns more rows than LEFT JOIN
quiz.explanation: A LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left table. Missing matches on the right produce NULL values for the right-side columns.

quiz.question:
What does this query return?

SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS task_count
FROM tasks
GROUP BY user_id;
options: One row containing the total number of tasks
One row for every task, with its user's total
One row for each user_id containing the number of tasks for that user
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY user_id creates one group per user_id, and COUNT(*) counts the tasks within each group.

options: It can update every row in the tasks table
It can only update task ID 1
It updates only rows where done is already 1
quiz.explanation: Without a WHERE clause, UPDATE applies to every row in the target table.

quiz.question: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY has calculated aggregates?
quiz.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results, often using aggregate expressions such as COUNT(*) or SUM(...).

exercise.title: Count open tasks for every user
exercise.task: Write ONE SQL query that returns every user, including users who have no tasks. Return exactly two columns: name and open_tasks. open_tasks must be the number of tasks belonging to that user where done = 0. Order the result first by open_tasks descending and then by name ascending. The database schema uses tasks.user_id as a foreign key to users.id. The exercise runs in SQLite, but the query should use standard SQL that also works in PostgreSQL.
exercise.setup:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE users (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE tasks (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    due_date TEXT
);

INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES
    (1, 'Anna'),
    (2, 'David'),
    (3, 'Maria'),
    (4, 'Peter');

INSERT INTO tasks (id, user_id, title, done, due_date) VALUES
    (1, 1, 'Learn SQL', 0, '2026-10-10'),
    (2, 1, 'Build API', 1, '2026-10-12'),
    (3, 1, 'Write tests', 0, NULL),
    (4, 2, 'Create controller', 0, '2026-10-08'),
    (5, 2, 'Add validation', 0, '2026-10-09'),
    (6, 2, 'Review code', 1, NULL),
    (7, 2, 'Document API', 0, '2026-10-15'),
    (8, 3, 'Design database', 1, '2026-10-06'),
    (9, 3, 'Create migration', 1, '2026-10-07'),
    (10, 3, 'Run tests', 1, NULL);
exercise.starter:
SELECT
    name,
    0 AS open_tasks
FROM users;
exercise.solution:
SELECT
    u.name,
    COUNT(t.id) AS open_tasks
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN tasks AS t
    ON t.user_id = u.id
   AND t.done = 0
GROUP BY u.id, u.name
ORDER BY open_tasks DESC, u.name ASC;
exercise.hint: Start from users because every user must appear. Use LEFT JOIN so a user without tasks is preserved. Put the done = 0 condition in the JOIN so completed tasks do not match while the user row is still kept. Then COUNT(t.id), GROUP BY the user, and order by the calculated count descending and name ascending.
